kabaddi.e: Borrowed from Hindi कबड्डी (kabaḍḍī), from Tamil கபடி (kapaṭi), from Tamil கைபிடி (kaipiṭi), from கை (kai, “hand”) + பிடி (piṭi, “catch, grasp”), which could be…

kabuki.x: The whole "weapons of mass destruction" concern was phony from the start, and the drama about inspections was just kabuki: going through the motions.

kaddish.e: Borrowed from Hebrew קַדִּישׁ (kadish, “kaddish”), from Aramaic קַדִּישׁ (qaddīš, “holy; holy person”). Doublet of kiddush.

kaftan.e: Via Russian кафта́н (kaftán), from Ottoman Turkish قفتان (kaftan), from Classical Persian خَفْتَان (xaftān), which occurs already in the Shahnameh.

kakapo.x: Analyses of the DNA fragments preserved in the moa and kakapo coprolites showed that moa and kakapo fed on fungi.

kaleidoscope.x: My heart fluttered like a kaleidoscope of butterflies, accompanied by an ocean of joyful tears.

kamikaze.e: Borrowed from Japanese 神風(かみかぜ) (kamikaze, “divine wind”), from 神(かみ) (kami, “divine”) + 風(かぜ) (kaze, “wind”).
kamikaze.x: Only top-shelf liquor is served, though Sasha refuses to serve drinks he deems fratlike. These include woo woos, kamikazes and shots of any kind.

kangaroo.e: Borrowed from Guugu Yimidhirr gangurru (“eastern grey kangaroo”). Despite a popular misconception, the Guugu Yimidhirr term does not mean "I don't know".

kanji.e: Borrowed from Japanese 漢字(かんじ) (kanji, “Chinese characters”), from Middle Chinese 漢 (MC xanH, “Han dynasty, China”) + Middle Chinese 字 (MC dziH, “[written] character”)…
kanji.x: Japanese is written in a mixture of kanji and kana.

kaolin.e: From French kaolin, François Xavier d'Entrecolles's irregular romanization of the Mandarin pronunciation of Chinese 高嶺土 /高岭土 (gāolǐngtǔ, “Gaoling earth”), from 高嶺 /高岭…

kapok.e: Borrowed from Malay kapuk (“silky fibre from the silk-cotton tree; Ceiba pentandra”).
kapok.x: You can stuff them full of kapok to make a decent cushion and there is nothing better to carry frogs in.

kappa.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek κάππα (káppa), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *kapp- (“palm, hand”). Doublet of kaph.
kappa.x: It was not quite possible for a kappa to go pale, but this one managed, shrinking partly into its shell.

karma.e: Borrowed from Sanskrit कर्म (kárma), nom.sg. of कर्मन् (kárman, “act, action, performance”).
karma.x: ‘We are all part of a circle of karma. We will be rewarded for the good deeds of our forefathers, and pay the price for their sins.’

kasha.e: Borrowed from Russian ка́ша (káša, “porridge, gruel”) or Yiddish קאַשע (kashe).
kasha.x: Some cooks add nuts as well, and I like the way their flavor complements that of the kasha and the browned onions.

katakana.e: From Japanese 片(かた)仮(か)名(な) (katakana).

katara.e: Borrowed from Hindustani کَٹَار (kaṭār) / कटार (kaṭār, “dagger, saber”).

katydid.e: Onomatopoeic, from the sound a common true katydid (Pterophylla camellifolia) makes by stridulating. * katydid song: (file).
katydid.x: In the night the katydids and crickets screeched in waves, soft then loud, back and forth.

kebab.e: Ultimately from Arabic كَبَاب (kabāb), partly through Hindustani (Hindi and Urdu), Punjabi, Persian and Turkish kebap. Doublet of cevapi. See the Arabic entry for more.
kebab.x: Let's go to the kebab after the club.

keelson.e: Late Middle English kelswayn, from Low German kielswîn, kielswīn, from kiel (“keel of a ship”) (from Old Norse kjǫlr) + swin (“swine”), used as the name of a timber…

keeper.e: From Middle English kepere. By surface analysis, keep + -er.
keeper.x: "Okay, that's a keeper," Harold said as he netted the 3-pounder and put him on a stringer over the side of the boat.

keepsake.x: Clam-shells are fashionable keepsakes. You write your name and the date inside one and your friend writes hers in the other and you exchange.

kefir.e: Borrowed from Russian кефи́р (kefír); see that entry for more.
kefir.x: Water kefir grains differ from milk kefir grains and are generally used to make kefirs based on fruit juices or sugared waters.

kelvin.e: Named after Irish-born Scottish physicist William Thomson, Lord Kelvin.
kelvin.x: The dew point here today is only 1 kelvin above what it was yesterday.

kendo.e: Borrowed from Japanese 剣道 (kendō, “the way of the sword”), from Middle Chinese 劍 (kjæ̀m, “sword”) + 道 (dáu, “way”). Doublet of kumdo.

kennel.e: PIE word *ḱwṓ From Middle English kenel, kenell, borrowed from Anglo-Norman *kenil, northern variant of Old French chenil, from Vulgar Latin *canīle, from Latin canis.
kennel.x: – We want to look at the dog kennels. – That's the pet department, second floor.

keratin.e: Borrowed from German Keratin, from Ancient Greek κέρας (kéras, “horn”) + -in. Doublet of carat.

kerchief.e: From Middle English keverchef, coverchef et al., from Old French couvrechief, from couvrir (“to cover”) + chief (“head”). Compare curfew.

kernel.x: The Dirichlet kernel convolved with a function yields its Fourier series approximation.

kestrel.e: From Middle English castrel (“staniel, bird of prey”), from Middle French cresserelle, crecerelle (“bird of prey”), usually assumed to be from crecelle (“rattle, wooden…
kestrel.x: When she was musing she was a kestrel, which hangs in the air by an invisible motion of its wings.

ketamine.e: Blend of ketone + amine. First use appears c. 1966.
ketamine.x: He was riding high that night, with a brick of Wage's ketamine on its way to Yokohama and the money already in his pocket.

ketone.e: From German Keton, from Aketon (“acetone”), from French acétone (“acetone”). See acetone.

kettle.e: From Middle English ketel, also chetel, from Old English ċietel (“kettle, cauldron”) and in Middle English possibly influenced by Old Norse ketill and both from…
kettle.x: To cook pasta, you first need to put the kettle on.

keycard.e: From key (“lock opener”) + card (“piece of plastic”).

keypad.x: Many laptop computers have special function keys which turn part of the alphabetical keyboard into a numeric keypad.

keystone.e: From key + stone. Definition 4 (retail) possibly originated in the jewelry industry in the magazine called "Jewelers' Circular-Keystone".
keystone.x: The tunnel, which is 1,000 yd. long, had been closed to passenger traffic since November 17, 1949, after some of the keystones had worked loose.

keyword.x: Each function has an entry address which must be quoted after the USR keyword.

khaki.e: Borrowed from Hindustani خاکی (xākī) / ख़ाकी (xākī), from Classical Persian خَاکِی (xākī, “dusty, earthy, earth-colored”).
khaki.x: The very loose seroual trousers were made in both sand-khaki drill, and in winter-weight khaki wool for wear with the M1946 battledress blouse.

khanate.x: Sviatoslav had his own imperial ambitions, which led him to take an aggressive interest in the Christian khanate of Bulgaria.

kidnap.e: From kid + nap (“to nab; to grab”). Originally Thieves' cant, referring to the practice of stealing children and shipping them to colonies or plantations as laborers.

kielbasa.e: Borrowed from Polish kiełbasa (“sausage”), from Proto-Slavic *kъlbasa, which may derive from Proto-Turkic for "grilled cutlet," literally "pressed on ashes," from *kül…

kimchi.e: Borrowed from Korean 김치 (gimchi), ultimately composed within Korea of Chinese-derived morphemes 沉 (MC drim, “submerged, soaked”) and 菜 (MC tshojH, “vegetable”), i.e.
kimchi.x: "Yeah." He gestured to the kimchi. "Well, get it in ya, then." "It's better hot." she said.

kimono.e: Borrowed from Japanese 着物(きもの) (kimono, “clothing”), which is from 着 (“wearing”) + 物(もの) (mono, “thing”).

kindergarten.e: Unadapted borrowing from German Kindergarten (“kindergarten”, literally “garden of children”), coined by German pedagogue Friedrich Fröbel in 1840.

kindle.e: From Middle English kyndelen, from Old Norse kynda (“to inflame”), from Proto-Germanic *kundijaną.
kindle.x: If a person kindle a fire in the house of another person, let him pay for the house to the owner, if it be burned.

kindred.e: From Middle English kyndrede, from older kynrede (“kindred”), from Old English *cynrēd, *cynrǣden (“kindred, family, stock”), from cynn (“kind, kin, lineage”) + -rǣden…
kindred.x: And what I wouldn't give to find a soulmate?/Someone else to catch this drift/And what I wouldn't give to meet a kindred?

kingfisher.e: Originally king's fisher, from Middle English kyngys fyschare; equivalent to king + fisher. So named for obscure reasons.

kingly.e: From Middle English kyngly, from Old English *cyninglīċ (“kingly, royal”), equivalent to king + -ly.
kingly.x: O thou dull god, why liest thou with the vile / In loathsome beds, and leav'st the kingly couch / A watch-case or a common 'larum-bell?

kingmaker.e: From king + maker, originally used in the 16th century in “Warwick the Kingmaker”, an epithet of Richard Neville, 16th Earl of Warwick (1428–1471), a key figure in the…

kingship.x: The traditional world knew divine kingship.

kinkajou.e: From French quincajou, from an Algonquian word, probably originally meaning ‘wolverine’ (compare Algonquin Kwingwaage, Ojibwe gwiingwa'aage (“wolverine”)), which was…

kinship.x: The first of these were the ten engines of class "C8", Nos.290-299, which had a very strong kinship to the C.R. "Carbrooks".

kinsman.e: From Middle English kynnesman, equivalent to kin + -s- + -man.
kinsman.x: And I, the nearest kinsman of the Earl of Windsor, was to propose his election.

kinswoman.e: From Middle English kynneswomman; equivalent to kin + -s- + -woman.

kiosk.x: I remember that one time I went to the kiosk next door to buy condoms, it was raining, she appeared.

kismet.e: From Ottoman Turkish قسمت (kısmet, “fate, destiny”) (Turkish kısmet), from Arabic قِسْمَة (qisma, “division, lot, destiny”).
kismet.x: But these things are kismet, and we only find out all about them just when any knowledge is too late.

kitchenette.x: It is a kind of large cellar with a kitchenette and a bathroomette adjoining.

kitsch.e: From German Kitsch, from dialectal kitschen (“to coat, to smear”).

kitten.e: From Middle English kitoun, kytton, kyton, keton (“kitten”), of obscure origin.

kleptomania.e: From Ancient Greek κλέπτω (kléptō, “to steal”) + -mania, analyzed as klepto- + -mania.
kleptomania.x: "He steals a lot?" "That's kleptomania," Sticky said.

kleptomaniac.e: From Ancient Greek κλέπτω (kléptō, “I steal”) (from Proto-Hellenic *klépt͏̌ō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *klep-) + -maniac.

knapsack.e: From Low German knapzak or Dutch knapzak (older form cnapsack), from Middle Dutch cnappen (“to bite with teeth”), ultimately from knappen (“to eat, crack”), of imitative…

knave.e: From Middle English knave, knafe, from Old English cnafa (“child, boy, youth; servant”), from Proto-West Germanic *knabō. Cognate to Dutch knaap and German Knabe.

kneel.e: From Middle English knelen, from Old English cnēowlian (“to kneel”), equivalent to knee + -le.
kneel.x: Kneel him down and stick his head in. No, don't let him up, just hold him there.

knickerbockers.e: From Knickerbocker + -s, after the short breeches worn by Diedrich Knickerbocker in George Cruikshank's illustrations of Washington Irving's 1809 A History of New York.

knighthood.e: From Middle English knyghthode, knyȝthod, from Old English cnihthād, from Proto-West Germanic *knehtahaidu, equivalent to knight + -hood.
knighthood.x: He's got an OBE and MBE, and his recent work should entitle him to a knighthood.

knitting.e: From Middle English knyttynge; equivalent to knit + -ing.
knitting.x: She put down her knitting and went to answer the phone.

knockoff.x: It's not a name-brand bag; it's just a cheap knockoff.

knockout.x: The boxer scored a knockout on his opponent.

knoll.e: From Middle English knol, knolle, from Old English cnoll (“summit”), from Proto-Germanic *knudan-, *knudla-, *knulla- (“lump”), possibly related to cnotta.
knoll.x: On knoll or hillock rears his crest, / Lonely and huge, the giant oak.

knotty.x: If thou murmur'ſt, I vvwill rend an Oake / And peg thee in his knotty entrailes, till / Thou haſt hovvl'd avvay tvvelve vvinters.

knowingly.e: From Middle English knawyngly, knowyngly. By surface analysis, knowing + -ly.
knowingly.x: She smiled knowingly, but kept the secret.

kofta.e: Borrowed from Classical Persian کوفْتَه (kōfta, “ground meat”), from کوفْتَن (kōftan, “to grind, break, beat”).

kohlrabi.e: Borrowed from German Kohlrabi, from Kohl (“cabbage”) + Italian rape (“turnips”), from cavoli rape, the plural of cavolo rapa (“cole rape”).

kombucha.e: Origin disputed. Possibly from Japanese 昆布茶 (konbucha, literally “kelp (konbu) tea”), a different type of beverage, and not related to fermentation.
kombucha.x: Kombucha is the primary focus of this book and arguably the most popular home ferment and aforementioned store-bought probiotic drink.

kopek.e: Borrowed from Russian копе́йка (kopéjka), from копьё (kopʹjó, “spear”) (from the image of a rider with a spear on the coins minted by Moscow after the capture of Novgorod…

kosher.e: Borrowed from Yiddish כּשר (kosher), from Hebrew כָּשֵׁר (kashér).
kosher.x: Only in New York can you find a good, kosher hamburger!

krill.x: “This science relates to krill and krill ecosystems, whale acoustic monitoring and Southern Ocean ecosystems,” the spokesperson said.

krone.e: From Danish krone (“crown”) and Norwegian krone. Doublet of corona, crown, korona, koruna, krona, and króna.

kryptonite.e: From a fictional radioactive element, kryptonite, that has a detrimental effect on the otherwise invulnerable character Superman.
kryptonite.x: The terrific seven-grain bread here is the kryptonite of restaurant reviewers: two mini-loaves and you are incapacitated.

kshatriya.e: From Sanskrit क्षत्रिय (kṣatriya, “(the warrior or military caste or a member of this caste”), from क्षत्र (kṣatra, “rule, dominion, authority”). Akin to satrap.

kugel.e: Borrowed from Yiddish קוגל (kugl), from Middle High German kugel(e) (“ball”), referring to the roundish appearance of some puddings. Further etymology uncertain.

kumquat.e: From Cantonese 金橘 (gam¹ gwat¹) or 金桔 (gam¹ gwat¹, literally “golden tangerine”). Related to loquat – same second character.

kurgan.e: From Russian курга́н (kurgán), from a Turkic language.

kurultai.e: Borrowed from Mongolian хуралдай (xuraldai) via Russian курулта́й (kurultáj).
